nutshell: New York is less a folk scene than the place where folk music was recorded, named, published and argued over, and it still runs on that history. In October 2026 the 23-county metro had roughly 410 participatory event-nights a month (about 325 counting only medium- and high-confidence listings). Irish sessions lead (78 to 141 a month), the legacy of the 1920s Sligo fiddlers whose Manhattan 78s standardized Irish music worldwide. Next comes a bar-and-brewery bluegrass circuit (about 70 jams a month) that dwarfs old-time (about 15). English country dance has run here since Cecil Sharp's 1915 visit, but contra is small for 20 million people (about 9 dances a month). Song lives in volunteer institutions (FMSNY, Peoples' Voice Cafe, NJ's Folk Project), a weekly Sacred Harp singing and harbor shanty sings, and Brooklyn's Jalopy anchors the roots revival. The heritage layer is vast: bomba, rumba, steelpan, rara, tassa, klezmer, Balkan brass, mariachi and powwows, much of it nurtured by CTMD since 1968.
signature_traditions: Irish traditional music (New York Sligo fiddle style, Comhaltas)
Sacred Harp and harbor shanty singing
Greenwich Village folk-song lineage (FMSNY, Peoples' Voice Cafe, Jalopy)

venues.notes: Hosts the FMSNY song circle and FMSNY concerts ($35 / $30 members, e.g. Oct 16 2026). BSEC moved here after selling its 53 Prospect Park West mansion for $13.5M in Dec 2023 (https://www.curbed.com/2023/12/brooklyn-society-for-ethical-culture-mansion-sold-poly-prep-park-slope.html). The old mansion was home to the Good Coffeehouse series.

venues.name: Folkus-NYC at Art Haus
venues.notes: Intimate unplugged series. Flagship Romance quote: 'One of the most intimate, yet acoustically pristine unplugged shows we've ever played.'

venues.name: Lincoln Road Center for the Performing Arts
venues.notes: House-concert-style Sundays at 4pm; reservations required; 'cat & dog in residence'. Fall 2026: Abby Newton & Selma Kaplan, Andy Statman Trio, Elias Ladino Ensemble.

venues.name: First Acoustics Brooklyn (backyard house concerts)
venues.place: Brooklyn (private home of Bruce & Coco Wilde)
venues.notes: Backyard concerts, 3pm, followed by a light supper. Not the same as First Acoustics in Kingston (Ulster Co., outside the MSA).

venues.name: Cowgirl Seahorse
venues.place: 259 Front St (at Dover St), South Street Seaport
venues.notes: Frequent 8pm folk, bluegrass and Americana bills (e.g. The Ramblin' Kind, Bluegrass by the Bridge); a Porch Stomp 2026 stage partner.

venues.name: Pete's Candy Store
venues.notes: Free back-room stage (Beth Orton played the first show; Will Oldham, Devendra Banhart and Norah Jones early). Singer-songwriter residencies.

venues.name: Joe's Pub (The Public Theater)
venues.notes: Cabaret and world/folk bookings (World Music Institute shows listed in the FMSNY newsletter).

venues.name: Main Drag Music (event space)
venues.notes: Instrument shop with an event space; 2026 residencies (e.g. London Plane).

venues.name: Cinema Arts Centre Sky Room
venues.notes: Home of the Hard Luck Cafe (since 1992) and NOOM; beer and wine available.

venues.name: Landmark on Main Street (Jeanne Rimsky Theater)
venues.place: 232 Main St, Port Washington, Nassau Co.
venues.notes: 8pm concerts plus free 'Afternoon T.E.A.' shows; John Platt cites it as a regular folk haunt.

venues.name: Our Times Coffeehouse (LI Ethical Humanist Society)
venues.place: 38 Old Country Rd, Garden City, Nassau Co.
venues.notes: First Fridays, open mic plus feature; $20 suggested.

venues.name: Walkabout Clearwater Coffeehouse (CUUC)
venues.notes: Run by the Walkabout Clearwater Chorus (a Clearwater sloop club with its own boat: https://walkaboutclearwater.org/). 2026-27 bill: Connie Kaldor, Matt Watroba & Robert Jones, Joe Crookston, Crys Matthews, Mustard's Retreat, Holly Near, Tom Chapin.

venues.name: Tompkins Corners Cultural Center
venues.place: 729 Peekskill Hollow Rd, Putnam Valley, Putnam Co.
venues.notes: Acoustic concerts (Rob Flax's Boom Chick Trio, Peppino D'Agostino, Oct 2026).

venues.name: Emelin Theatre
venues.notes: Listed by FMSNY as a regular folk-concert location.

venues.name: Caramoor (Rosen House Music Room series)
venues.notes: 2026-27 Rosen House Concert Series (Oct-May) includes Brooklyn indie-folk (Bandits on the Run).

venues.name: Turning Point
venues.notes: Started as a 36-seat restaurant room where local musicians played 'for passing the bottle'; named for a John Mayall album. A low-ceilinged basement room for folk, blues and singer-songwriters; booking into Dec 2026 (https://piermont.club/shop/).

venues.name: Morristown Unitarian Universalist Fellowship (Troubadour)
venues.place: 21 Normandy Heights Rd, Morris Township, NJ
venues.notes: New 300-seat hall; smoke- and alcohol-free; Kingston Trio and Jeff Daniels have sold it out.

venues.name: Outpost in the Burbs
venues.place: First Congregational Church, Montclair, Essex Co., NJ
venues.notes: Founded spring 1987 by young adults in the church library; a 501(c)(3) since 2001. Pairs concerts with volunteering (a monthly community kitchen in Orange). Suzanne Vega played Oct 30 2026.

venues.name: Hurdy Gurdy Folk Music Club (Fair Lawn Community Center)
venues.place: 10-10 20th St, Fair Lawn, Bergen Co., NJ
venues.notes: Normally 10 concerts a season on first Saturdays. Last dated item found: a May 2024 'ANNOUNCEMENT' event on Viewcy (https://www.viewcy.com/event/announcement); its old domain hurdygurdyfolkmusic.com no longer resolves. Current status unverified.

venues.name: Sanctuary Concerts
venues.notes: Yelp: about 450 seats in a church sanctuary, tickets around $25. Its former domain sanctuaryconcerts.org was serving an unrelated Vietnamese-language blog in Oct 2026. Status unknown, probably inactive.

venues.name: Towne Crier Cafe
venues.notes: Outside the MSA (Dutchess). Thursday open mic, 6:30pm.

organizations.name: Center for Traditional Music and Dance (CTMD)
organizations.kind: folk arts presenter, archive and community cultural initiative incubator
organizations.notes: Founded as the Balkan Arts Center by Martin Koenig (Ethel Raim co-director from the mid-1970s); renamed Ethnic Folk Arts Center (1981-98), then CTMD. Says it has founded seven 501(c)(3) cultural organizations, incl. the first East Coast youth academies for Mexican and Peruvian music and NY's main annual Dominican, Indo-Caribbean, Colombian and Albanian festivals; has assisted 20 NEA Heritage Fellows. Current Sustaining Cultures initiatives: Venezuelan, Himalayan, Inner Asian, An-sky Institute for Jewish Culture, Soorya NYC. Office 32 Broadway.

organizations.name: City Lore: New York Center for Urban Culture
organizations.kind: urban folklore center (People's Hall of Fame, Place Matters, People's Poetry Gathering)
organizations.notes: Founded by folklorist Steve Zeitlin; office at 56 E 1st St hosts Yiddish song gatherings and book launches (e.g. Zingeray, Oct 27, 2026; Sinuhé Padilla-Isunza's 'Son Jarocho Fandango', Oct 26, 2026). citylore.org blocked automated fetches.

organizations.name: Long Island Traditions
organizations.notes: Founding director Nancy Solomon retired; Violet Baron became executive director in early 2024. Covers singing, dance, storytelling, maritime occupational life.

organizations.name: Bronx Music Heritage Center / Bronx Music Hall (WHEDco)
organizations.notes: Permanent home in the Bronx Music Hall at Bronx Commons (ground broken 2017). Partners include City Lore, Garifuna Coalition and Los Pleneros de la 21; hosted LP21's 'Por la Plena' concert (June 6, 2026) and the Garifuna Collective (Aug 2025).

organizations.name: Los Pleneros de la 21 (LP21)
organizations.notes: Founded by Juan 'Juango' Gutiérrez with plenero Marcial Reyes Arvelo; named for 'Parada 21' in Santurce. Grammy-nominated (2006, with Tito Matos). Based at 1680 Lexington Ave (Julia de Burgos Latino Cultural Center). Annual Gran Fiesta Navideña, Fiestas de Cruz, Sancocho Musical; December parrandas through El Barrio.

organizations.name: Mariachi Academy of New York (MANY)
organizations.notes: Idea came from Queens father-and-son musicians Ramón Ponce Sr. and Jr. (Mariachi Real de México). Opened July 2002. 120 students per undated page.

organizations.name: New York Klezmer Series (NYKS)
organizations.kind: klezmer concert, workshop, jam and dance-party series
organizations.notes: Founded and curated by drummer Aaron Alexander, co-founded by Rabbi Greg Wall; 250+ evenings; weekly in seasons Sept 2010-Mar 2020, scaled back since 2023; fiscally sponsored by CTMD; at Hudson Yards Synagogue.

organizations.name: Yiddish New York
organizations.kind: annual Yiddish culture festival and community
organizations.notes: Successor to KlezKamp's December gathering; Dec 26-31 at the 14th Street Y (in person and on Zoom); billed as 'the world's largest annual gathering celebrating Yiddish culture' (CTMD).

organizations.name: Zlatne Uste Balkan Brass Band / Golden Festival
organizations.kind: Balkan brass band and festival producer
organizations.notes: Band founded 1983; created the Golden Festival in 1986 (began in a Manhattan loft); first foreign musicians to play Serbian music at the Guča brass festival (invited five times; featured in the documentary 'Brasslands').

organizations.name: Greek American Folklore Society (GAFS)
organizations.kind: Greek folk dance society and costume collection (Paul Ginis Costume Collection)
organizations.notes: Astoria; classes, performances, 'Vimata Eleftherias' Hellenic dance weekend (Mar 2026). Founding year inferred from its contact address; low confidence.

organizations.name: Pontian Society 'Komninoi' of New York
organizations.kind: Pontic Greek society and dance group
organizations.notes: 31-25 23rd Ave, Astoria. 1966 founding from the society's own Facebook description.

organizations.name: Omonoia Cretans Association of New York
organizations.notes: Astoria; affiliated with the Pancretan Association of America.

organizations.name: Society of Epirotes 'Anagenesis' / Heritage Museum of Epirus
organizations.notes: 25-14 Broadway, Astoria. Epirot clarinet tradition is that of NEA Fellow Periklis Halkias.

organizations.name: Dancing Crane Georgian Cultural Center
organizations.kind: Georgian cultural center and repertory company
organizations.notes: 302 Kings Highway, Brooklyn; calls itself the oldest Georgian cultural center in New York; founding director Victor Sirelson; men's choir Zekari directed by Paata Tsetskhladze.

organizations.name: Garifuna Coalition USA
organizations.notes: Founded in the Bronx; requested the first Garifuna-American Heritage Month proclamation (Bronx BP Adolfo Carrión Jr., Mar 11, 2009).

organizations.name: West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA)
organizations.notes: Runs Panorama behind the Brooklyn Museum and the Labor Day parade on Eastern Parkway (59th edition in 2026 per PIX11).

organizations.name: Thunderbird American Indian Dancers
organizations.kind: all-volunteer Native American dance company and scholarship fund
organizations.notes: Oldest resident Native American dance company in New York; founded by Native New Yorkers of Mohawk, Hopi, Winnebago, Seneca and other descent; director/emcee Louis Mofsie (Hopi/Winnebago); 350+ scholarships awarded.

organizations.name: American Indian Community House (AICH)
organizations.notes: Serves Native Americans in NYC; seasonal Governors Island space and artist residency (2026).

organizations.name: Lenape Center
organizations.notes: Led by Lenape elders incl. co-founder Joe Baker; fiscally sponsored by NYFA.

organizations.name: Éenda-Lunaapeewáhkiing Collective
organizations.notes: Founder George Stonefish; executive director Brent Stonefish (Ontario); organizes the United Lenape Nations Pow Wow (Armory 2018; Prospect Park 2025, 2026).

organizations.name: Chinese Music Ensemble of New York
organizations.notes: Founded by Tsuan-nien Chang (1917-1997); ~50 members (Wikipedia); 65th-anniversary concert at Carnegie Hall May 17, 2026.

organizations.name: Chinese Musical and Theatrical Association (CMTA)
organizations.notes: One of NYC's oldest amateur Cantonese opera clubs; members were often laundry and restaurant workers; archive at MOCA.

organizations.name: Mencius Society for the Arts
organizations.notes: CTMD Sharing Traditions partner.

organizations.name: Soh Daiko
organizations.notes: Organized Dec 1979 under the New York Buddhist Church; 'first taiko ensemble on the East Coast'; began 48th season fall 2026.

organizations.name: Korean Traditional Performing Arts Association
organizations.notes: Founded by NEA Fellow Sue Yeon Park after she immigrated in 1982.

organizations.name: Jalikunda: Home of the Griots
organizations.notes: Founded by Senegalese kora player Malang Jobarteh.

organizations.name: Cumbe: Center for African and Diaspora Dance
organizations.notes: Weekly sabar, Haitian, West African, Congolese, Afro-Brazilian classes in Fort Greene, Brooklyn.

organizations.name: Pachamama Peruvian Arts
organizations.notes: Incorporated Apr 24, 2008 (NY company registry); free after-school program.

organizations.name: FolkCOLOMBIA Escuela de Danza y Música
organizations.notes: Jackson Heights.

organizations.name: University of the Philippines Alumni & Friends Rondalla (UPAFR)
organizations.notes: New Jersey; free Sunday-afternoon rondalla lessons for all ages in Central Jersey. Founding year from the site's '1995-2026' copyright line; low confidence.

organizations.name: Polish Highlander Alliance of New Jersey, Group No. 6
organizations.notes: Part of the Polish Highlanders Alliance of North America (founded 1929 in Chicago). Picnic in Clifton NJ.

organizations.name: New Amsterdam Musical Association (NAMA)
organizations.kind: African American musicians' association and jam venue
organizations.notes: Described as the oldest African American musical organization in the US; brownstone at 107 W 130th St.

organizations.name: Hālau Hula O Nā Mele 'Āina O Hawai'i
organizations.notes: Opened May 1968 under Luana Haraguchi; now teaches through Brooklyn Conservatory of Music.

organizations.name: Brooklyn Arts Council Folk Arts program
organizations.notes: First folklorist Kathleen Condon; Dr. Kay Turner 2000-2014; Christopher Mulé to 2020, when BAC ended the program. Produced Brooklyn Maqam, Harborlore, Folk Feet, Half the Sky festival.

organizations.name: World Music Institute
organizations.notes: Still presenting in 2026 (Minyo Crusaders' NYC debut, Sultan Room, Sept 22, 2026).

organizations.name: Queens County Farm Museum
organizations.kind: historic farm; host of the Thunderbird powwow
organizations.notes: Calls itself the longest-running presenter of Native American arts and culture in NYC.

organizations.name: Flushing Town Hall
organizations.notes: Multilingual programming; monthly jazz jams; Diwali Festival 2026.

organizations.name: Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, Mid-Atlantic Region
organizations.notes: Ten branches listed in 2026 (NYC, Queens/Brooklyn, Bronx-Westchester-Rockland, Long Island, two in NJ, Philadelphia, Baltimore/DC, Pittsburgh, SE Florida); Boston College's finding aid lists twelve, including Claddagh na nGael (Jersey Shore) and Rialta Cheol (central NJ), which no longer appear. Runs the Mid-Atlantic Fleadh and a Hall of Fame (since 1990).

organizations.name: Mulligan-Quinn Branch CCÉ
organizations.notes: Nassau & Suffolk. Founded 1972-73 as the Louis Quinn Branch, 'the oldest branch of Comhaltas in North America', after the Irish Music Association (president Bill McEvoy) merged into CCÉ; renamed mid-1990s for fiddler John Columbcille Mulligan. Monthly céilís at Mineola.

organizations.name: Craobh Úll Mór Nua Eabhrac CCÉ
organizations.notes: New York City branch; ran a weekly Sunday guest-led session (Blaggard's, then Seven Bar & Grill, then Mustang Harry's, 2004-2007+) and Irish language classes at NYIC.

organizations.name: Killoran-Clancy-Whelan Branch CCÉ
organizations.notes: Queens & Brooklyn; named in part for fiddler Paddy Killoran.

organizations.name: Coleman-O'Grady Branch CCÉ
organizations.notes: Bronx, Westchester and Rockland; descends from the 1950s Michael Coleman Club in the Bronx (ITMA).

organizations.name: Martin Mulvihill Branch CCÉ (Pearl River School of Irish Music)
organizations.notes: Northern NJ & Rockland; teachers Margie Mulvihill, Patty Furlong, Rose Conway Flanagan, Brenda Dowling; sends students to Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann; ran Uncle Tommy's Pearl River seisiúns (2025).

organizations.name: Rafferty-Madden Branch CCÉ
organizations.notes: Central & northern NJ; named for flute player Mike Rafferty and (presumably) accordionist Joe Madden.

organizations.name: Irish Arts Center
organizations.notes: Classes in fiddle, concertina, harp, bodhrán, whistle, mixed instruments, dance, Irish language; Bill Ochs Scholarship Fund. Nye Heron directed it 1976-2021.

organizations.name: New York Irish Center
organizations.notes: See venues.

organizations.name: Glucksman Ireland House NYU
organizations.notes: Founded by Lewis Glucksman; music programming under Mick Moloney.

organizations.name: Royal Scottish Country Dance Society, New York Branch
organizations.notes: Group began after a Scottish Nationality Weekend at Michael Herman's Folk Dance House in March 1954; class from fall 1955 taught by Jeannie Carmichael commuting from Boston; became the RSCDS's second official US branch in May 1959 (after Boston, 1950). Runs Pawling Weekend (since 1963), Jeannie Carmichael Ball, Burns Night.

organizations.name: RSCDS New Jersey Branch
organizations.notes: Members 'in their teens and in their 90s'.

organizations.name: Westchester Scottish Country Dance Society
organizations.notes: Wednesday classes in Elmsford.

organizations.name: Saint Andrew's Society of the State of New York
organizations.notes: Founded Nov 19, 1756 'for the relief of Natives of Scotland'; first president Philip Livingston, later a signer of the Declaration of Independence.

organizations.name: New York Caledonian Club
organizations.notes: Runs Scottish fiddle and traditional music workshops (e.g. Mary Abdill, Oct 2024, $35/$40; earlier Matthew Christian, Calum Pasqua) and marches in the Tartan Day Parade; records at the New-York Historical Society.

organizations.name: Society of the Friendly Sons of St. Patrick in the City of New York
organizations.notes: Founded March 17, 1784 by Irish officers of the Continental Army; supports IAC education programmes today.

organizations.name: Irish American Association of Northwest Jersey
organizations.notes: Rockaway Township; slow + regular sessions monthly since 2005; harp, set dancing, language classes.

organizations.name: Bergen Irish Association
organizations.notes: Dumont NJ; Monday set dancing.

organizations.name: Blarney Star Productions (Don Meade)
organizations.notes: Concert series lineage from the Eagle Tavern (first session June 10 1975); Meade has run it since 1986.

organizations.name: Ceol Agus Rince Promotions (Maureen Donachie)
organizations.notes: East Coast calendar of sessions, céilís and concerts, Maine to Florida; daily emails reach 'nearly 2,000'; Donachie is a world-champion step dancer and set dancer.

organizations.name: Grafton Street Open Irish Session (GSOIS)
organizations.notes: Long Island group running rotating monthly sessions (Smithtown, Center Moriches, Mount Sinai, formerly Westhampton Beach) since the Grafton Street Pub days.

organizations.name: Cat and Fiddle Sessions
organizations.notes: NJ/Brooklyn session organisation of Tony Horswill and Tom Dunne (Dorrian's 2003, St James's Gate, O'Connell's, Jack O'Neill's, now The Hutton).

organizations.name: Brooklyn Traditional Slow Jam
organizations.notes: Slow jam with master tune list.

organizations.name: New York Sean Nós Dance Club
organizations.notes: Alice Breda Ryan and Christine Timm; classes and workshops.

organizations.name: New York Irish History Roundtable
organizations.notes: Publishes New York Irish History (e.g. John T. Ridge, 'Dance Halls of Irish New York', vol. 19, 2005).

organizations.name: Gaelic Athletic Association of New York
organizations.notes: Owner of Gaelic Park.

organizations.name: Michael A. Flanagan Irish Music Heritage Inc.
organizations.notes: Sponsored a Catskills Irish Arts Week 2026 concert (Irish Echo via CIAW site); details not found.

organizations.name: Irish Echo
organizations.notes: Weekly with Dan Neely's traditional-music column and a tri-state events listing; 1920s-30s rival The Advocate (James Hayden's 'In Irish Circles' column) is the best source for the 78 era.

organizations.name: Country Dance New York (CDNY)
organizations.kind: contra & English dance society; CDSS affiliate
organizations.notes: All-volunteer 501(c)(3); 'we and our predecessors have been putting on dances in NYC for 100 years'. Lineage: NYC branch of the English Folk Dance Society set up after Cecil Sharp's 1915 visit (https://cdss.org/about/history/). Yelp lists 'Established in 1916'. Two dances a week Sep-early June.

organizations.name: Country Dance & Song Society (CDSS)
organizations.notes: 1915 US branches of the EFDS (Boston first, then NY, Chicago, Pittsburgh); 1933 EFDSSA formed with national HQ in New York City under May Gadd; renamed Country Dance Society 1949, '& Song' 1967. (Now headquartered in Massachusetts.)

organizations.name: Brooklyn Contra (Traditions Unlimited)
organizations.notes: Almost entirely volunteer; explicitly political framing of 'participatory folk culture' quoting Pete Seeger; runs the Five Borough Fling weekend and a Substack ('The View From The Balcony').

organizations.name: Village Contra
organizations.notes: Bills itself as 30+ years of gender-free contra in NYC; relaunched fall 2026.

organizations.name: Long Island Traditional Music Association (LITMA)
organizations.notes: Incorporated Sep 18 1980; contras, English dance, house sings & potlucks. litma.org was blocked as 'malware' by this research environment's corporate web filter, so its pages were read only via search snippets and CDSS. | Monthly house sing (Rise Up Singing), contras at Smithtown's Brush Barn, orchestra rehearsals. Its website was unreachable in Oct 2026; information from the FMSNY newsletter.

organizations.name: The Folk Project
organizations.notes: Incorporated 1976 (founded early 1970s as Project 21 by Laurie Riley; roots in 1966 Thirsty Ear coffeehouse, https://www.njskylands.com/cl_folkproject_113). Runs Swingin' Tern contras (since 1984), Troubadour concerts, festivals. Song thread covers concerts. | Began as Project 21 (Laurie Riley, 1973); incorporated 1976. Runs the Troubadour (weekly since 1975), Open Stage, Streaming Tuesdays, Inside the Song (Zoom), the Swingin' Tern contra and the spring Acoustic Getaway, and absorbed the Big Orange Tarp artist community. 500 paid members, up 66% in a few years (Morristown Green, 2025).

organizations.name: Bluegrass & Oldtime Music Association of New Jersey (BOTMA)
organizations.notes: Founded 1978 by nine friends at informal pickin'; also distributes the monthly 'All Jam No Spam' NJ jam calendar (Aileen Krupa).

organizations.name: Bluegrass Club of Long Island (BCLI)
organizations.notes: 501(c)(3) 'in its 40th year'; co-presents the Long Island Bluegrass & Roots Music Festival with BACCA.

organizations.name: Westchester Bluegrass Club
organizations.notes: Monthly Sunday shows with pre-show jam/open mic in Purdys; connects players with teachers.

organizations.name: Pinelands Cultural Society (Albert Music Hall)
organizations.notes: Incorporated Oct 4 1975 'to collect and preserve the cultural history of the people... of the pinelands'.

organizations.name: Scandia New York / New York Spelmanslag
organizations.notes: Began in the 1980s (https://nordstjernan.com/news/east/2772/).

organizations.name: City Stompers
organizations.notes: Artistic director Megan Downes (ex-Footworks Percussive Dance Ensemble); 'New York City's only clogging school'.

organizations.name: Times Squares Square Dance Club
organizations.notes: Founded Oct 1984; 'largest LGBT-and-friends social square dance club in the country' (Meetup) and NYC's only square dance club (own site).

organizations.name: Half Moon Sword
organizations.notes: Hosts the New York Sword Dance Festival (Ale) since 1986.

organizations.name: Ring O'Bells Morris
organizations.notes: 'Oldest women's Morris side in North America'; 50th season at NEFFA 2025; founded 1974 per Brooklyn Promenade video caption.

organizations.name: Bouwerie Boys Morris Dancers
organizations.notes: Founding year not found.

organizations.name: Griggstown Lock (morris)
organizations.notes: Listed as active NJ side by NAMDO (Griggstown is in Somerset County); no details verified. NAMDO lists Millstone River Morris (Princeton) as ceased though PCD's page still describes it.

organizations.name: Country Dancers of Westchester (CDW)
organizations.notes: Co-founded by choreographer Fried de Metz Herman (centenary of her birth marked Nov 2026).

organizations.name: Brooklyn Heights International Folk Dancers
organizations.notes: Elaine Sohn 30+ years.

organizations.name: Monmouth Folk Dancers
organizations.notes: 60+ years; hosted a New Jersey Folkdance Fest (10th annual listed).

organizations.name: Israeli Dance Institute
organizations.notes: Presents the annual Israel Folk Dance Festival (74th in 2026, Hunter College).

organizations.name: Jim's Roots & Blues / New York Bluegrass (nybluegrass.com) / Bluegrass Jams Near Me / Start Jamming
organizations.notes: Jim's began 2010 as an NYC bluegrass/old-time calendar; nybluegrass.com runs a public Google calendar (116 entries) maintained by a volunteer with a Venmo tip jar.

organizations.name: Folk Music Society of New York (New York Pinewoods Folk Music Club)
organizations.kind: folk society (CDSS affiliate, Folk Alliance member)
organizations.notes: All-volunteer. Monthly newsletter (vol. 61 in 2026; 11 issues a year) with the region's most complete folk calendar. Runs song circles, concerts, the Fall Weekend (first NYC-based edition Oct 2025) and TradMaD camp at Pinewoods. Reciprocal discounts with LITMA, Princeton FMS, CD*NY, BKCM and Brooklyn Contra. ~150 members per the Oct 2026 newsletter. 2026 president Clarice Kjerulff.

organizations.name: Folk Music Society of Huntington (FMSH)
organizations.notes: Founded in the late 1960s, incorporated 1970; membership was once 'in the hundreds'. From Oct 1 2026 it stopped presenting all public events. The Hard Luck Cafe passed to the Cinema Arts Centre and the library jam became the Pidgeon Hill Acoustic Folk Jam.

organizations.name: NYC Sacred Harp
organizations.notes: Weekly Manhattan singing, monthly Brooklyn (Joe Beasley) singing, monthly seven-shape singing, and the NYC All-Day Singing (Sept; 177 registered in 2026). Founding year inferred: the 2007 all-day was the '3rd session' (https://fasola.org/minutes/search/?n=2656).

organizations.name: Sacred Harp of Central New Jersey
organizations.notes: New Brunswick; held a Central NJ All-Day Singing (2nd annual in 2014: https://www.princeton.edu/~gibney/SacredHarp/2014CNJADS_flyer.pdf).

organizations.name: Jalopy Theatre & School of Music / Living Traditions
organizations.notes: Produces the Brooklyn Folk Festival (2009-) and the Washington Square Park Folk Festival (2011-); Jalopy Records; Jalopy Chorus.

organizations.name: Porch Stomp
organizations.kind: festival organization (fiscally sponsored by Make Music New York)
organizations.notes: 100% volunteer; also runs Flatfoot Flatbush and Jam Face. Producer Theo Boguszewski ('aspiring fiddler').

organizations.name: People's Music Network for Songs of Freedom and Struggle - NYC Chapter
organizations.notes: First-Friday song swaps, showcases, and the Winter Gathering in NYC (Jan 23-25 2026, Central Park East II School).

organizations.name: Greenwich Village Folk Festival Association
organizations.notes: Founders Rod MacDonald, Ray Micek, Jay Rosen, Gerry Hinson. Annual concerts 1987-94; monthly online concerts Jul 2020-Dec 2024; 40th-anniversary concert at Cooper Union, Oct 4 2026.

organizations.name: Walkabout Clearwater Chorus
organizations.kind: community folk chorus and coffeehouse (Clearwater sloop club)
organizations.notes: Coffeehouse since 1989, now in White Plains.

organizations.name: Hudson River Sloop Clearwater
organizations.notes: HQ in Beacon (Dutchess, outside the MSA). Ran the Great Hudson River Revival at Croton Point (Westchester) from 1978 until 2020 (virtual 2021). Now runs the Folk Picnic in Beacon, music sails and the 2026 60th-anniversary concert series.

organizations.name: Harper House Music Foundation / RiverFest For Pete's Sake
organizations.notes: Produces the Hudson River Music Festival at Croton Point Park (2025-); helped donate Revival artifacts to the NYS Museum.

organizations.name: New York City Labor Chorus
organizations.notes: Singers from 20+ unions; 35th-anniversary concert May 2 2026 at Adler Hall with the Resistance Revival Chorus; auditions Nov 16 2026.

organizations.name: The New York Packet
organizations.notes: Official maritime singing group of the South Street Seaport Museum, 'established over 30 years ago', first singing aboard Peking; its members host the 1st-Sunday chantey sing.

organizations.name: Noble Maritime Collection
organizations.notes: Snug Harbor, Staten Island; monthly Doerflinger memorial shanty sessions co-sponsored by FMSNY.

organizations.name: Big Orange Tarp
organizations.kind: artist-support community (now under the Folk Project)
organizations.notes: Founded by Alan Rowoth. Showcases at every NERFA, 20+ years of Folk Alliance showcases, and the early folk listserv 'long before wifi'.

organizations.name: New Folk Initiative
organizations.notes: John Platt's platform: playlists, curated concert calendar, On Your Radar previews.

organizations.name: Outpost in the Burbs
organizations.kind: nonprofit concert presenter and volunteer org
organizations.notes: Montclair NJ.

organizations.name: Hurdy Gurdy Folk Music Club
organizations.notes: Status after May 2024 unverified (see venues).

organizations.name: Peoples' Voice Cafe collective
organizations.notes: Not affiliated with any political or religious organization.

festivals.name: Zlatne Uste Golden Festival
festivals.notes: 40th edition Jan 16-17, 2026 at The Marquee Astoria (formerly Astoria World Manor), Queens; Friday dance teaching + party, Saturday 5 stages and 40-60 bands. Bills itself as North America's largest Balkan music & dance festival.

festivals.name: Yiddish New York
festivals.notes: 14th Street Y; workshops by day, concerts by night, film festival, kids' program. CTMD lists the 2026 edition as the '13th annual'; first visual-arts exhibition was 2015.

festivals.name: Shinnecock Indian Nation Powwow
festivals.notes: 80th annual Sept 4-7, 2026, Southampton (Suffolk); $50,000+ in drum and dance prizes; adult admission $20. archives.notes: 64.8 linear feet, 1986-2013 bulk: program files, audiovisual documentation and oral histories (Brooklyn Maqam, Harborlore, Folk Feet, Praise in the Park).

archives.notes: Annotated Cantonese opera scores, scripts, correspondence, photographs and recordings, 1930s-1980s; digitized as 'Tunes Near and Far'.

archives.notes: New York City: Global Beat of the Boroughs (2001), Badenya: Manden Music in New York City (2002), Quisqueya en el Hudson: Dominican Music in New York (2004); plus a Shashmaqam (Bukharian) album.

archives.notes: Henry Sapoznik and Adrienne Cooper on KlezKamp's creation and growth.

archives.name: Lomax Digital Archive / Association for Cultural Equity (Hunter College, Manhattan)
archives.notes: Alan Lomax's own nonprofit, chartered in New York in 1983 and housed at Hunter College's fine arts campus; its free online archive includes field sessions recorded in New York City, e.g. Aunt Molly Jackson (May 1939, disc AFS 2579) and Jean Ritchie (1949-50), plus Lomax's radio shows. Originals of the pre-1942 recordings are at the Library of Congress.

archives.name: Library of Congress, American Folklife Center: Alan Lomax collection (AFC 2004/004) and Archive of Folk Song discs
archives.notes: Holds the 1939 New York recordings of Aunt Molly Jackson and Lomax's correspondence with her; Lead Belly also recorded for the Library in the early 1940s while living in New York. A Kentucky project has put the 1939 Aunt Molly sessions online.

archives.name: Library of Congress AFC: Israel G. 'Izzy' Young collection (AFC 2015/040)
archives.notes: Acquired December 2015: scrapbooks, journals, correspondence, photographs and recordings from the Folklore Center (110 MacDougal St, 1957-1973) and the Stockholm Folklore Centrum; a day-by-day paper trail of the Village revival.

archives.name: Library of Congress AFC: Center for Traditional Music and Dance collection
archives.notes: Documents CTMD from its 1968 founding by Martin Koenig as the Balkan Arts Center through its Ethnic Folk Arts Center (1981) and CTMD (1997) phases.

archives.name: Library of Congress AFC: Seeger family collections
archives.notes: Seeger family members are documented in 58 AFC collections (thousands of manuscript pages, about 1,100 sound recordings), including David Dunaway's 1976-1983 interviews with Pete Seeger and contemporaries (AFC 2000/019).

archives.name: Ralph Rinzler Folklife Archives and Collections / Smithsonian Folkways (Washington, DC)
archives.notes: The Moses and Frances Asch Collection: the business files and masters of New York's Folkways Records (2,168 titles), bought by the Smithsonian in 1987 after negotiations led by Passaic-raised Ralph Rinzler. The single biggest repository of New York-made folk recordings.

archives.name: Tony Schwartz sound documentaries (Folkways)
archives.notes: Eleven Folkways LPs by the New York sound archivist, beginning with 'New York 19' (1954), recorded inside one Manhattan postal zone: street songs, immigrant music, children's games. 'New York Taxi Driver' is in the National Recording Registry.

archives.name: The Cradle of Harmony: William Sidney Mount's Violin and Fiddle Music (Folkways, Gilbert Ross, 1976)
archives.notes: Tunes from the Mount manuscripts played on one of Mount's surviving patent violins; Mount's own 'In the Cars on the Long Island Railroad' is the only original composition.

archives.name: Long Island Museum of American Art, History & Carriages (Stony Brook): William Sidney Mount collection
archives.notes: Largest repository of Mount's art and papers, including his hand-written music manuscripts (estimates of 'hundreds' to 450+ tunes, c. 1840s-1860s, some with dates and sources such as Shepard Jones), his 'Spirit Journal', and two of his 'Cradle of Harmony' violins (the 1852 patent form and the more conventional 1857 shape); the Smithsonian's NMAH holds another (sources count three or four surviving versions). Exhibitions: Catching the Tune (1984), The Power of Music (2002), Perfect Harmony (2018). Thirty of the tunes were published by Alan Buechner and Bill Shull for the museum.

archives.name: William Sidney Mount and Mount family papers (Archives of American Art, Smithsonian)
archives.notes: Papers 1830-1947 (bulk 1830-1860) from the New-York Historical Society and the Suffolk Museum at Stony Brook; notes that brothers Robert, Henry and Shepard and sister Ruth were 'also artistic and musical'.

archives.name: NYU Archives of Irish America (Tamiment Library): Mick Moloney Irish-American Music and Popular Culture Collection
archives.notes: Five-part collection (papers, commercial recordings, Irish Americana, etc.) spanning 1817 to the present; one of the largest US collections for Irish-American music and popular culture.

archives.name: ITMA 'From The Bridge': Irish traditional music in New York (online exhibition)
archives.kind: online archive/exhibition (Irish Traditional Music Archive, Dublin)
archives.notes: Chapters from the 1870s (piper Patsy Touhey, Brooklyn-born accordionist John Kimmel) through the 78-rpm age (Coleman, Morrison, Killoran), post-war (Catherine Brennan-Grant, the New York Céilí Band), the revival (Eagle Tavern & Blarney Star, Joanie Madden, Billy McComiskey) and today (Dylan Foley, Rose Flanagan); collections from Louis Quinn, Terry Rafferty, Charlie Mulvihill and Don Meade.

archives.name: New York Public Library for the Performing Arts: Rodgers and Hammerstein Archives of Recorded Sound
archives.notes: Grew from Columbia's 1937 gift of 500 78s; a separate division since 1965 at Lincoln Center. NYPL's Dance Division also holds the Michael and Mary Ann Herman papers (Folk Dance House).

archives.name: City Lore archive (Lower East Side)
archives.notes: Founded 1986; more than 100,000 images, hundreds of oral histories, and traditional music and poetry performance tapes; feeds the online 'City of Memory' story map.

archives.name: Irwin Silber Collection (UNC Southern Folklife Collection, Chapel Hill)
archives.notes: Papers of the Sing Out! editor (1951-1967) and People's Songs veteran: correspondence, song books, interviews, newsletters.

archives.name: Woody Guthrie Archives (now Woody Guthrie Center, Tulsa)
archives.notes: Kept in Mount Kisco, Westchester, by Nora Guthrie until 2013; more than 10,000 items (typed lyrics, notes, illustrations, recordings, photos), much of it from his New York years. Bought by the George Kaiser Family Foundation in 2011.

archives.name: Library of Congress: Federal Writers' Project life histories and folklore (B. A. Botkin)
archives.notes: Botkin, national folklore editor of the FWP (1938-39) and later head of the Archive of American Folk Song, directed the life-history and folklore interviews, which include New York City material; Botkin lived in Croton-on-Hudson (Westchester) until his death in 1975. NYC-specific holdings not itemized in this pass.

archives.name: Discography of American Historical Recordings (UCSB)
archives.notes: Session-level data for the New York-made 78s: Michael Coleman (1921-1936), Eck Robertson (1922), Pawlo Humeniuk and others; the best way to see how many fiddle records were cut in Manhattan studios.

archives.name: Herbert Halpert's New York and New Jersey fieldwork
archives.notes: Halpert's Columbia MA thesis was 'Folk Rhymes of New York City Children' and his Indiana PhD 'Folktales and Legends of the New Jersey Pines'. Where his field recordings now sit was not verified here.

archives.name: Teresa Rafferty videotapes
archives.notes: Decades of house sessions in Mike Rafferty's NJ basement plus festival/concert footage, digitised at ITMA; 'one of the most important sources of live recordings' in the exhibition.

archives.notes: Scottish club records since 1856.

timeline.event: Colonial New York and New Jersey newspapers run fugitive-slave advertisements describing enslaved people who 'play on the fiddle'; Hodges & Brown's anthology Pretends to Be Free lists nearly one hundred fiddlers among the runaways, the earliest large body of evidence for fiddling in the region.

Pinkster (Dutch Pentecost) becomes a major African American festival with dancing and drumming; by the mid-1700s celebrations in New York and Brooklyn draw very large crowds of enslaved and free Black people.
Saint Andrew's Society founded in New York (Nov 19), first president Philip Livingston: the oldest Scottish society in the city.
Society of the Friendly Sons of St. Patrick founded (March 17) by Irish officers of the Continental Army.

'Staten Island Hornpipe' first printed, in James Aird's Selection (vol. II, Glasgow); the title may refer to the British garrison on Staten Island during the Revolution (one theory) or to Isla de los Estados off Cape Horn.
The Easy Instructor, the first shape-note tunebook, is compiled by William Smith (very likely of Hopewell NJ) and William Little.
The New-Brunswick Collection of Sacred Music is published (8 editions to 1841).

Enslaved and free Black Long Islanders and New Jerseyans who sell produce at Catharine Market (Lower East Side) 'dance for eels' on shingles for fish and coins, the scene later described in Thomas De Voe's The Market Book (1862) and cited as a root of tap and of blackface minstrelsy's stolen steps.

Micah Hawkins, New York tavern-keeper, fiddler-composer and uncle of William Sidney Mount, stages The Saw-Mill, or A Yankee Trick at the Chatham Garden Theatre, called the first opera by an American composer on an American theme.

William Sidney Mount shows 'Rustic Dance After a Sleigh Ride' at the National Academy of Design, the first of his Long Island dance paintings (later 'Dancing on the Barn Floor' 1831, 'The Dance of the Haymakers' 1845, 'Right and Left' 1850, 'The Banjo Player' 1856).

'Zip Coon', the minstrel tune later known as 'Turkey in the Straw', is published and popularized by New York blackface performer George Washington Dixon (authorship also claimed by Bob Farrell and George Nicholls).

Charles Dickens visits Almack's dance hall at 67 Orange Street in Five Points and describes 'the corpulent black fiddler, and his friend who plays the tambourine' playing a 'regular break-down' for a brilliant young dancer, usually identified as Master Juba (William Henry Lane).

Feb 6: the Virginia Minstrels (Dan Emmett on fiddle, Billy Whitlock banjo, Frank Brower bones, Dick Pelham tambourine) debut at the Bowery Amphitheatre, the first full-evening blackface minstrel show; the fiddle-banjo-bones-tambourine band became the template that carried fiddle tunes nationwide.
July 8: Master Juba and the white dancer John Diamond meet in a $200 challenge dance at the Bowery Amphitheatre, as advertised in the New York Herald.
Famine-era immigration: many Irish arriving at New York 'never got farther west than the Hudson River', giving New York the largest Irish population of any US city.

Jan 7: Mount copies 'Merry Girls of New York' (noted 'Composed by T. Ntt.') into his tune manuscripts at Stony Brook, one of hundreds of dance tunes the painter-fiddler collected from neighbors and print.

Dec 4-5: at Stony Brook, Mount writes out 'In the Cars on the Long Island Railroad', the one tune in his manuscripts known to be his own composition (recorded by Gilbert Ross on Mount's own violin for Folkways).
June 1: William Sidney Mount is granted a patent for his hollow-backed 'Cradle of Harmony' violin, designed to be heard over the noise of country dances.
Mount demonstrates and plays the Cradle of Harmony at the New York Crystal Palace exhibition; the juries pronounced all violins 'unfit for competition'.
February: Mount notes 'Shep Jones Hornpipe' from his Setauket neighbor and fellow fiddler Shepard Jones, one of the few named local sources in the manuscripts.
James A. Bland, later composer of 'Oh, Dem Golden Slippers' (1879, now a fiddle and Mummers standard), is born on Long Island to a family of free Black people.
New York Caledonian Club founded.
April 4: 'Dixie', composed in New York by fiddler Dan Emmett, is first performed by Bryant's Minstrels at Mechanics' Hall, New York City.
New York Illustrated News pictures a slum dance hall where dancers do 'a wild jig', an early image of Irish dance in the city.
Thomas F. De Voe's The Market Book records the Catharine Market eel-dancing tradition, the main written source for it.
Landmark Tavern opens on the Hudson waterfront (home of a Monday session since 2006).
Step dancer Kitty O'Neil stars with Harrigan & Hart at the Theatre Comique; Irish musicians and dancers dominate variety and vaudeville.

Music publishers cluster on West 28th Street, the start of 'Tin Pan Alley', which turns New York into the country's song-publishing center (songs and sheet music, though the big fiddle-tune books came from Boston and Chicago).
Our Lady of Mount Carmel Feast and the 'Dancing of the Giglio' begin in Williamsburg (Nola-rooted Italian feast with a band riding the tower).
Leitrim-born Ellen O'Byrne and her Dutch-American husband Justus DeWitt open their Irish music shop in Manhattan, later called 'the founding mother of the Irish record industry'.
New Amsterdam Musical Association founded; it later settles in its Harlem brownstone and still hosts weekly Monday jams.
Uilleann piper Patsy Touhey records (c.1904), among the earliest Irish traditional recordings made in New York.

Harding's Music House, New York, issues Harding's All-Round Collection of Jigs, Reels and Country Dances (200 tunes for piano, violin, flute or mandolin), a New York counterpart to Boston's Ryan's/Howe collections (IMSLP date for the scanned edition).

Mike Donovan opens Donovan's Hall at Columbus Circle, credited as New York's first large Irish dance hall; county-named halls proliferate in the 1920s-30s (Galway Hall and others make 125th Street a center of Irish entertainment by 1930; Brooklyn's Harp of Erin, 1932).
Dance Hall License Act's $50 fee wipes out many back-room Irish halls.

Cecil Sharp comes to New York as dance consultant for a production of A Midsummer Night's Dream; American branches of the English Folk Dance Society begin that year, the root of today's Country Dance and Song Society, whose national office stayed in New York City until 1987.
Sligo fiddler James Morrison emigrates to New York; he wins the New York Feis fiddle competition in 1918 and becomes one of the city's leading Irish music teachers in the 1930s-40s.
Cecil Sharp's US visit; branches of the English Folk Dance Society formed (Boston first, then New York, Chicago, Pittsburgh) - root of today's CDNY.
Intertribal powwows begin in Prospect Park, Brooklyn (held through 1972).

Sept 15: after Justus DeWitt Jr. recruits players at Sunday open-air sessions at Celtic Park (Queens, then described as on Long Island), O'Byrne DeWitt persuades Columbia to record Irish dance music, guaranteeing to buy the records; 'The Stack of Barley' is among the first sides.
Cardinal Farley bans church-sponsored dances, boosting commercial Irish dance halls.
Michael Coleman, after arriving in America in October 1914 and touring vaudeville, settles in New York City.
Otto Heinemann's OKeh label (New York studio and pressing plant) begins issuing records, including German, Czech, Polish, Swedish and Yiddish lines for immigrant buyers.
Klezmer violinist-bandleader Abe Schwartz copyrights about 35 tunes ahead of a new round of recordings; his 'Di Grine Kuzine' becomes a lasting hit of the New York Yiddish record trade.
Michael Coleman's first disc (c.1920) on piper Tom Ennis's Shannon label, with 'Reidy Johnson's Reels'.
Michael Coleman makes his first commercial recordings in New York (Shannon and Vocalion); by 1936 he cuts about 80 sides whose re-export to Ireland reshaped Irish fiddling.
James Morrison and the Flanagan Brothers (Dec 1921) begin recording; the 1920s make New York 'the Irish music capital of the world' and its 78s 'a de facto national standard' back in Ireland.
June 30-July 1: Texas fiddler Eck Robertson (with Henry Gilliland) records 'Arkansaw Traveler' and 'Sallie Gooden' for Victor in New York, widely called the first commercial country records.
Redie Johnston becomes the first female Irish traditional musician on a commercial record (Gennett).

March 7-8: Georgia fiddler Gid Tanner and Riley Puckett record for Columbia in New York, its first country artists; Ernest Stoneman (Sept) and Uncle Dave Macon with fiddler Sid Harkreader (July 8) also make their first records in NYC that year.
New York-based singer Vernon Dalhart records 'The Wreck of the Old 97'/'The Prisoner's Song' for Victor, reputedly the first country record to sell a million.
May 19: Sligo fiddler Paddy Killoran lands in New York; he settles at first in East Harlem and becomes, with Coleman and Morrison, the third great Sligo-in-New-York recording fiddler.
July 27: Charlie Poole and the North Carolina Ramblers (fiddler Posey Rorer) record 'Don't Let Your Deal Go Down Blues' for Columbia after auditioning in New York City.

Dec 3: Ukrainian-born New York fiddler and violin maker Pawlo Humeniuk begins recording for OKeh; 'Ukrainske Wesilia' (Ukrainian Wedding, 1926) reportedly sold 100,000-150,000 copies and his Polish 'Kanarek' (1928) became the era's best-selling polka.
GAA of Greater New York buys Gaelic Park in the Bronx.
Roscommon-born fiddler Larry Redican emigrates to New York; a prolific tune-finder and composer, he dies on Jan 26, 1975 while playing on stage at the Irish American Society in Mineola, Long Island.
Irish Echo founded.

November: Meyer Horowitz opens the Village Barn on West 8th Street, a country-music nightclub with square dancing; from 1948 to 1950 NBC broadcasts 'Village Barn' from it, the first country music program on American network television, with caller Piute ('Plute') Pete among the regulars. The site later became Jimi Hendrix's Electric Lady Studios.
Chinese Musical and Theatrical Association, an amateur Cantonese opera club for laundry and restaurant workers, founded in Chinatown.

December: Kentucky singer and union activist Aunt Molly Jackson comes to New York to raise money for striking Harlan County miners and stays, becoming a link between Appalachian song and the city's left-wing folk circle.
Pride of Erin Ballroom opens in Brooklyn: 30,000 sq ft of maple floor for 2,000 dancers; Irish immigration then almost stops for the Depression.
English Folk Dance and Song Society of America formed with national HQ in New York City; May Gadd national director.
Coleman records the 'Bonnie Kate/Jennie's Chickens' and 'Tarbolton' sets; WLWL's 'Smiles and Tears of Erin' (1934-37) broadcasts live Irish bands.
Jan 1: Lead Belly arrives in New York with John Lomax; newspapers seize on the 'singing convict'. His East 10th Street apartment later becomes a gathering place for Guthrie, Seeger and others.
Feb 22: Max Gordon opens the Village Vanguard, which presents folk music (Lead Belly, calypso by the Duke of Iron) and poetry until it turns to jazz in 1957.

Columbia Records gives 500 78-rpm discs to the New York Public Library's Music Division, the seed of what became the Rodgers and Hammerstein Archives of Recorded Sound (separate division from 1965 at Lincoln Center).

Barney Josephson opens Café Society at 2 Sheridan Square, a nightclub that treated Black and white customers alike and a home for Josh White, Lead Belly's circle, gospel quartets and boogie-woogie; it closes in 1948 after red-baiting of Josephson's brother.
May: Alan Lomax records Aunt Molly Jackson's ballads, sacred songs and reminiscences in New York City for the Library of Congress Archive of Folk Song.
Michael & Mary Ann Herman teach folk dance at the New York World's Fair.

February: newly arrived Woody Guthrie writes 'This Land Is Your Land' in New York; on March 3 he meets Pete Seeger at Will Geer's 'Grapes of Wrath Evening' benefit. That year Lomax and Nicholas Ray's CBS radio show 'Back Where I Come From' features Guthrie, Lead Belly, Josh White, Burl Ives, Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee.

Ukrainian-American violinist Michael Herman leads folk dancing for passers-by at the American Common of the New York World's Fair; on Oct 15 he and Mary Ann Herman open a folk dance center in the Ukrainian National Home on East 6th Street, which grows into Folk Dance House.
Oct 15: Hermans open a folk dance center at the Ukrainian National Home, E. 6th St (later Folk Dance House on 16th St).

The Almanac Singers (Seeger, Lee Hays, Millard Lampell, then Guthrie) form in New York; at Almanac House they hold Sunday 'hootenannies', a word Seeger and Guthrie had picked up that summer on tour in Seattle and Portland. On May Day they sing 'Talking Union' to 20,000 striking transit workers at Madison Square Garden.

Lead Belly is introduced to Moses Asch, whose small New York label (Asch Records) issues three Lead Belly albums between 1941 and 1944; Asch also records Guthrie's 'This Land Is Your Land' in April 1944.
Dec 10: Oscar Brand's 'Folksong Festival' debuts on WNYC; it runs until September 2016, the longest-running radio show with a single host per Guinness.

Dec 31: People's Songs is founded in New York by Pete Seeger, Alan Lomax, Lee Hays and others to 'create, promote, and distribute songs of labor'; its Bulletin runs 1946-1950 and its hootenannies spread the form.
Michael Coleman dies (Jan 4) and is buried in St. Raymond's, Bronx.
1940s: Washington Square Park becomes a Sunday gathering place for folk singers (Seeger, Guthrie).
First annual Shinnecock Pow Wow, Southampton.

Post-war Sunday-afternoon folk singing at the Washington Square fountain becomes a fixture; banjoist Roger Sprung, who first heard folk music in 1947, is among the mid-1950s regulars interviewed in the first issue of The Village Voice.
Moses Asch and Marian Distler found Folkways Records in New York; by Asch's death (1986) it has issued 2,168 titles of world, folk, children's and documentary recordings.

Lomax records Kentucky ballad singer Jean Ritchie in New York City (1949-50); Ritchie, then a social worker at the Henry Street Settlement, later lives for decades in Baxter Estates/Port Washington, Long Island.
Name changes to Country Dance Society ('and Song' added 1967).
The Weavers, after a steady engagement at the Village Vanguard, top the charts for 13 weeks with Lead Belly's 'Goodnight, Irene' on Decca; within two years they are blacklisted.
Post-war Irish dance-hall era: the Tuxedo Ballroom (E. 86th St and Third Ave), City Center (155 W. 55th St) and Jaeger House (E. 85th and Lexington) become the focal points of Irish weekend dancing.
Sing Out! (May), Vanguard and Elektra are all founded in New York.
Tom and Paddy Clancy arrive in Greenwich Village as actors; with Liam Clancy (1956) and Tommy Makem they become the Clancy Brothers, who brought Irish ballad singing to the Village coffeehouse scene.
Folkways issues Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music, a compilation of commercial 78s from 1926-1932 assembled by the New York-based collector, and the 'bible' of the coming revival.
Early 1950s: Roger Sprung brings Southern bluegrass banjo to Washington Square; Allan Block's W 4th St sandal shop becomes an old-time jam hub.
Tony Schwartz's Folkways LP 'New York 19' documents the folk and street music of a single Manhattan postal zone (today's 10019/10036).

Clare accordionist Joe Cooley moves to the US and leads the Joe Cooley Céilí Band in New York before moving on to Chicago and San Francisco; New Jersey's Luke O'Malley credits Cooley and Paddy O'Brien with popularizing 'The Sally Gardens' reel around New York.
A Scottish Nationality Weekend at Folk Dance House launches Scottish country dancing in New York.
December: the blacklisted Weavers reunite for a sold-out Carnegie Hall concert; Vanguard's 1957 LP of it helps ignite the late-1950s folk boom. Seeger and Hays testify before HUAC the same year.
Israel 'Izzy' Young opens the Folklore Center at 110 MacDougal Street, a shop, concert room and message board for the revival; he produces Bob Dylan's first concert (Carnegie Chapter Hall, 1961).

The New Lost City Ramblers (Mike Seeger, John Cohen, Tom Paley) form in New York to play old-time string band music learned from 78s and field trips. The Gaslight Cafe and the Village Gate open the same year.
New York Céilí Band formed (Paddy O'Brien, Redican, McGann, Reynolds, Coen, Felix Dolan); Tulla Céilí Band plays Carnegie Hall and Martin Mulhaire stays.
Manny Roth opens Cafe Wha? in a former horse stable at 115 MacDougal Street.
New York group becomes the RSCDS's second official US branch (May).
Greenbriar Boys form out of Washington Square jams.
1960s: Sunday rumba takes root in Central Park (first Puerto Rican players at Bethesda Fountain, later Cuban), a meeting ground during the civil-rights and Young Lords years.
Jan 26: Mike Porco's Gerdes restaurant at 11 West 4th Street becomes a music room (The Fifth Peg, with Izzy Young); on June 1 it is reborn as Gerdes Folk City.
NY Céilí Band places third at Fleadh Cheoil in Boyle; Paddy O'Brien, Jack Coen and Larry Redican win the trio title.
Chinese Music Ensemble of New York founded by Tsuan-nien Chang.

January: Bob Dylan arrives in New York (visiting Woody Guthrie at Greystone Park hospital in Morris County, NJ); April 11 he plays his first professional gig at Gerdes Folk City, opening for John Lee Hooker.

Feb 11: the Friends of Old Time Music (John Cohen, Ralph Rinzler, Izzy Young, with Jean Ritchie and Margot Mayo as 'board') present their first concert, Roscoe Holcomb with Ritchie, the Greenbriar Boys and the NLCR, at P.S. 41 in the Village; March 25 brings Clarence Ashley with Doc Watson, and fiddler Gaither Carlton.
April 9: the 'Beatnik Riot' at Washington Square after Parks Commissioner Newbold Morris refuses the folksingers' Sunday permit; Izzy Young leads the protest and the singing eventually returns.
Fred Weintraub opens The Bitter End at 147 Bleecker Street (still operating; it bills itself as New York's oldest rock club).
Sis Cunningham and Gordon Friesen start Broadside, the mimeographed topical-song magazine that first printed many Dylan and Ochs songs.
Thunderbird American Indian Dancers founded by Native New Yorkers.
Peter Stampfel and Steve Weber form the Holy Modal Rounders on the Lower East Side, reworking old-time fiddle-and-banjo tunes with absurdist humor.
Bob Fass's Radio Unnameable starts on WBAI; Pete Wernick starts WKCR's bluegrass programming.
Postcrypt Coffeehouse opens under St. Paul's Chapel, Columbia.

Feb 12: at an FOTM concert in New York, Maybelle Carter shares the bill with Sam and Kirk McGee and the Tennessee fiddler Arthur Smith; FOTM's last concert is May 14, 1965. The same year Bronx-born Andy McGann makes his first LP, 'A Tribute to Michael Coleman', and Connemara singer Joe Heaney settles in New York after Newport.
Immigration Act cuts Irish arrivals to about 500 a year; Tuxedo Ballroom closes; McGann, Burke & Dolan record 'A Tribute to Michael Coleman'.
New York Pinewoods Folk Music Club (now FMSNY) founded by Pinewoods Camp enthusiasts as a CDSS division.
Pontian Society 'Komninoi' founded in Astoria.

Pete and Toshi Seeger found Hudson River Sloop Clearwater; in 1969 the sloop's maiden voyage ends at South Street Seaport in Manhattan, and the organization's Great Hudson River Revival festival follows.
Kathleen Collins becomes the first American-born senior All-Ireland fiddle champion.
Martin Koenig founds the Balkan Arts Center (now CTMD), after Ethel Raim asks why no Newport performers 'had accents'; hālau hula opens in an Upper East Side apartment (May).
American Indian Community House founded; Balkan Arts Center launches its Spring (1969-77) and Winter (1969-85) Folk Festivals.

After Bronx-raised Ethel Raim asks Ralph Rinzler why no Newport performers had immigrant accents, immigrant performers she documented appear at the 1969 Newport Folk Festival and then at the Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife.
City Center Ballroom and Jaeger House gone as Irish dance halls; Tower View, Woodside, is the last big one.
Folk Music Society of Huntington incorporated.
The Gaslight Cafe on MacDougal Street, opened 1958 as a 'basket house', closes.
Martin Mulvihill emigrates to the Bronx and starts his school.
Irish Arts Center founded by Brian Heron on E 13th St; Louis Quinn Branch of CCÉ formed in Mineola (1972-73), the first in North America.
Early 1970s: Folk Dance House building demolished.
Izzy Young closes the Folklore Center and moves to Stockholm, where he runs the Folklore Centrum until 2018.
Fordham students launch WFUV's Ceol na nGael.
Ring O'Bells (oldest women's morris side in North America) and Country Dancers of Westchester founded; Albert Music Hall's weekly Saturday shows begin in Waretown (Nov).
New Jersey Folk Festival founded at Rutgers by Angus Gillespie; Thunderbird dancers begin their Theater for the New City partnership.
First Eagle Tavern Monday session (June 10) on West 14th St, started by dissidents from the Irish Arts Center's Monday sessions (American Irish Cultural Project); Shanachie Records founded.
July 25: first show of the series that becomes the Minstrel/Troubadour ($1, about 25 seats, French-restaurant basement in Chester NJ).
Casita Rincón Criollo built in the South Bronx; CTMD's Queens Ethnic Music and Dance Festival begins (to 1991).

New Jersey flute player Mike Rafferty (from Ballinakill, Co. Galway; NEA Heritage Fellow 2010) is among a group of New York-area Irish musicians invited to the Smithsonian's Bicentennial Festival of American Folklife.
Mick Moloney brings Jack Coen to the Smithsonian bicentennial festival; Fr. Charlie Coen wins three All-Irelands in one day.
Turning Point opens in Piermont; Folk Project incorporates.
Bulgarian singing recorded by Koenig and Raim flies on the Voyager Golden Record.

Mick Moloney co-founds the Green Fields of America touring ensemble; in December the Songwriters Exchange begins meeting at the new Cornelia Street Café (opened July 1977), the seed of the 1980s 'new folk' scene.
Cornelia Street Cafe opens; Carolyne Mas starts a songwriters' night there in December.
Bluegrass & Oldtime Music Association of NJ founded.
Clearwater folk picnics take root as the Great Hudson River Revival at Croton Point.
Soh Daiko, the East Coast's first taiko group, organized at the New York Buddhist Church (December).
Peoples' Voice Cafe founded by Songs of Freedom and Struggle members.
Mariel boatlift brings a new generation of Cuban rumberos who reshape Central Park rumba.
Long Island Traditional Music Association incorporated (Sep 18).
Ron Olesko creates Traditions on WFDU.
Frisner Augustin forms La Troupe Makandal (Haitian Vodou drumming), led until his death in 2012.
Half Moon Sword founded.
Hurdy Gurdy Folk Music Club founded in Fair Lawn NJ.

February: Fast Folk Musical Magazine (first called The CooP) begins; until 1997 it issues 98 releases with 1,389 tracks, first recordings for Suzanne Vega, Shawn Colvin, Lyle Lovett, John Gorka and others.
John Nolan becomes the first American senior All-Ireland button accordion champion.
Los Pleneros de la 21 formed (Juan Gutiérrez, Marcial Reyes Arvelo); Zlatne Uste Balkan Brass Band founded.
Bronx fiddle teacher Martin Mulvihill (born Co. Limerick 1923; teacher of Eileen Ivers) and Brooklyn klezmer clarinetist Dave Tarras are named NEA National Heritage Fellows.
Joanie Madden wins senior All-Ireland whistle; Martin Mulvihill becomes an NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Swingin' Tern contra (Folk Project) first dance Jan 7; Times Squares square dance club founded Oct.
KlezKamp begins (Catskills, outside the MSA); CTMD's Bronx project produces Cherish the Ladies' first album.
Mick Moloney's 'Cherish the Ladies' concert of young women players (Ethnic Folk Arts Center) spawns the band.
SideWalk Cafe opens on Avenue A; Lach conceives the Antifolk Festival.
City Lore founded; Zlatne Uste starts the Golden Festival in a Manhattan loft.
Brian Conway wins senior All-Ireland fiddle; Kathleen Biggins begins A Thousand Welcomes; around 1986-87 Koch-era Cabaret Law enforcement ends Friday céilí dancing at the Eagle.
First New York Sword Dance Festival; Bluegrass Club of Long Island founded.
Gerde's Folk City closes (March).

The Smithsonian acquires Folkways Records from the Asch family (negotiated by Ralph Rinzler), moving the label to Washington; Gerdes Folk City loses its lease and closes; CDSS moves its national office from New York City to western Massachusetts.
Greenwich Village Folk Festival and Outpost in the Burbs both founded.
Brooklyn Arts Council starts a NYSCA-funded Folk Arts program (ended 2020).
Walkabout Clearwater Coffeehouse begins.
Peruvian Parade and Festival begins in Paterson; NEA honors Calabrian musicians Giuseppe and Raffaela DeFranco of Belleville NJ.
After the Happy Land Social Club fire in the Bronx, the city enforces fire rules in music venues; the Eagle Tavern's back room is rebuilt down to 60 capacity.
Andy McGann honorary president of the Fleadh in Sligo; CCÉ Mid-Atlantic Hall of Fame begins (first inductee Tom Doherty, Mineola). Happy Land fire forces the Eagle back room down to 60 seats.
Long Island Traditions founded.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann's North American convention in Secaucus, NJ inspires Canadian flutist Jean Duval's reel 'The Caucus Reel' ('The Caucus at Secaucus').
NYC Labor Chorus founded.
Shashmaqam master Ilyas Malayev arrives in Rego Park (Oct); Fatima Kuinova and Ng Sheung-Chi named NEA Heritage Fellows.
Hard Luck Cafe begins in Huntington.
Antifolk settles into the back room of the SideWalk Cafe on Avenue A, home of the annual New York Antifolk Festival until 2019.
Eagle Tavern shut without notice (Dec) as rents rise; concerts move to Tony Brady's Blarney Star, Tribeca; Glucksman Ireland House founded at NYU.
First Garden State Sacred Harp Convention, Montclair (shape-note revival in NJ from the early 1990s).
Giuliani-era 'quality of life' policing: police confiscate Central Park rumba drums; rumberos play bodies, benches and coolers for about two years.
February: the Village Gate (opened 1958 at Bleecker and Thompson) closes its Greenwich Village location.
Big Orange Tarp founded (Alan Rowoth); Living Traditions founded.
Catskills Irish Arts Week founded in East Durham (Don Meade, artistic director).
John Platt takes over WFUV's Sunday Breakfast; Fast Folk ends.
Garifuna Coalition USA founded in the Bronx; Sidiki Conde forms Tokounou All-Abilities ensemble.
Pete's Candy Store opens in Williamsburg.
Blarney Star, two blocks from Ground Zero, sealed off after 9/11; concerts move briefly to the IAC.
Mariachi Academy of New York opens in East Harlem (July); Folkways releases CTMD's 'Badenya: Manden Music in New York City'.
Blarney Star sold and renamed Biddy Early's; concerts move to Washington Square Methodist Church (2004), then Glucksman Ireland House.
The 'Blarney Star' concerts move to Washington Square United Methodist Church (sold to a condo developer within six months), then to NYU's Glucksman Ireland House, paid for at Mick Moloney's urging.
New York Irish Center opens in Long Island City.
Radio Jarocho begins promoting son jarocho and the fandango in New York.
Michael Daves starts the First Monday Bluegrass Jam at Rockwood Music Hall.
First NYC Sacred Harp singing (2007 = '3rd session'); Rockwood Music Hall opens.
Jalopy Theatre opens in Red Hook; Dave Harvey launches the monthly NYC Barn Dance (Oct).
Dust Busters (later Down Hill Strugglers) form; Feral Foster's Roots n' Ruckus moves from the Village Ma to Jalopy.
First Garifuna-American Heritage Month proclaimed in the Bronx; Lenape Center founded.
First Brooklyn Folk Festival.
New York Klezmer Series begins weekly seasons (to March 2020).
Brooklyn Contra founded.
Washington Square Park Folk Festival founded; Rick Snell starts Mona's Monday bluegrass.
Hurricane Sandy (Oct 29) burns down the Harbor Light Pub, Belle Harbor, home of a Rockaway session.
Hurricane Sandy floods Sunny's (reopens Sept 2013); Andy Statman named NEA National Heritage Fellow.
The Woody Guthrie Archives, kept by Nora Guthrie in Mount Kisco (Westchester) and bought in 2011 by Tulsa's George Kaiser Family Foundation, move to the new Woody Guthrie Center in Tulsa.
Dead Rabbit's Sunday seisiún and the Iona Scottish session begin.
CDNY contras move from the Chinatown YMCA (Bowery) to Church of the Village (Feb 2).
Jan 27: Pete Seeger, born in Manhattan in 1919, dies; Sing Out!, born in New York in 1950, publishes its last print issue in spring 2014.
First Porch Stomp on Governors Island (inferred from 13th edition in 2026).
Porch Stomp founded (Make Music NY); Sunnyside Singers Club starts weekly; Sing Out! ends as a print quarterly.
Yiddish New York festival begins as KlezKamp's December successor; Pan Evolution Steel Orchestra founded.
December: the Library of Congress American Folklife Center acquires the Israel G. Young collection (Folklore Center and Folklore Centrum papers, scrapbooks, recordings).
The Living Room closes (Dec 21).

Oscar Brand's WNYC Folksong Festival ends after almost 71 years (Brand dies Sept 30, 2016). Brooklyn-born accordionist Billy McComiskey, composer of 'The Flowers of Brooklyn', is named an NEA National Heritage Fellow.
NYC's Cabaret Law dancing ban, which had shut the Eagle's céilís, finally repealed; Lillie's Union Square Saturday session ends Oct 7.
Mandolin Brothers (Staten Island) and Matt Umanov Guitars (Bleecker St) close their retail stores.
First United Lenape Nations Pow Wow at the Park Avenue Armory.
Caffè Vivaldi closes (June); last recorded Garden State Sacred Harp Convention.
Jalikunda: Home of the Griots founded by kora player Malang Jobarteh.
Hank's Saloon, Brooklyn's honky-tonk dive, closes for good (June).
Cornelia Street Cafe closes (Jan 2; rent had gone from $450 to $33,000/month); SideWalk Cafe closes after its final Winter Antifolk Festival (Feb); Folk Music Notebook launched.
COVID ends the NY Klezmer Series' weekly run (March); Brooklyn Arts Council drops its Folk Arts program.
COVID-19 shuts New York's small music rooms; in April the Jalopy's owners join other independent venues banding together to survive the closures.
COVID ends the Blarney Star series at NYU (March); pubs close; Lambertville session pauses until 2022.
COVID: dances suspended; CDNY runs online events; CDW 'Zoom in the New Year'; CDW's first post-pandemic dance Oct 3 2021.
COVID: the Clearwater Revival ends its traditional form; GVFF moves to monthly online concerts; the Folk Project streams and raises $140,000 for performers.
New $60M Irish Arts Center opens on Eleventh Ave (Dec 8); Joanie Madden named NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Bob Fass dies (Apr 24); the Clearwater Revival is virtual for its final year.
Mick Moloney dies (July); Blarney Star concerts revived at the New York Irish Center; Moriarty's Yonkers Sunday seisiún begins.
ITMA publishes 'From the Bridge', a digital exhibition on Irish music in New York.
Woody's Children ends on WFUV after 54 years (Jan 29); Brooklyn Society for Ethical Culture sells its Park Slope mansion (Dec), the former Good Coffeehouse home.
Casita Rincón Criollo listed on the National Register of Historic Places; Violet Baron succeeds Nancy Solomon at Long Island Traditions.
Happy Traum, a Bronx-born Washington Square regular of the late 1950s, dies (July 17). The Rutgers American Studies department ends its run presenting the New Jersey Folk Festival (1975-2024).
Fr. Charlie Coen dies (Dec 26); Laurels session starts; Harold Dunn, Lambertville session leader of 25+ years, dies (April).
Sam Ash closes all stores; Rockwood Music Hall closes abruptly (Nov 10); first Clearwater Folk Picnic in Beacon.
Peniel Guerrier (Haitian dance and drum, Astoria) named NEA Heritage Fellow; Lenape powwow returns to Prospect Park, the first there since 1972; NJ Folk Festival turns 50.

Historic Hudson Valley's Pinkster Festival ('Remembrance and Renewal', May 24) at Philipsburg Manor, Sleepy Hollow (Westchester) keeps the colonial Afro-Dutch spring holiday alive with drumming, dance and storytelling.
First Hudson River Music Festival at Croton Point; the Troubadour turns 50 with membership at 500; FMSNY holds its first NYC-based fall weekend; the Brooklyn Folk Festival runs in November.
Golden Festival's 40th (Jan); Pan Evolution's third straight Panorama title (Sept 5); 80th Shinnecock Pow Wow; first Albanian Festival on Staten Island; CTMD launches its Joseph Moskowitz archive.

The Brooklyn Folk Festival announces its 2026 lineup (including the New York City-born old-time fiddler Bruce Molsky with Michael Daves and Tony Trischka); the New Jersey Folk Festival relocates to South Brunswick.
Cherish the Ladies become the first US-based group to win TG4's Gradam Ceoil group award; Uncle Tommy's in Pearl River closes; new sessions open in Brooklyn, Highland Park and Midtown.

Jalopy burgled (June 15), community covers losses; Village Contra relaunches; BKCM holds its first Old Time Square Dance (May); 40th NY Sword Dance Festival; Brooklyn Folk Festival & Five Borough Fling share Nov 6-8.

Feb 15: the last Sunday Supper on WFUV. The Owl Music Parlor announces its closure. Oct 1: FMSH exits public presenting. The GVFF holds its 40th-anniversary concert and Jalopy marks 20 years. The NYS Museum opens its Clearwater Revival exhibit.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Merry Girls of New York
tunes_named_for_city.notes: In William Sidney Mount's manuscripts, dated Stony Brook, Jan 7, 1849, with the note 'Composed by T. Ntt.'

tunes_named_for_city.title: In the Cars on the Long Island Railroad
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Mount's only known original composition, written out at Stony Brook Dec 4-5, 1850; recorded by Gilbert Ross on Mount's own violin (Folkways). Probably the first fiddle tune about a Long Island commute.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Shep Jones Hornpipe
tunes_named_for_city.notes: From Mount's Setauket neighbor and fellow fiddler Shepard Jones, February 1854: a tune named for a Long Island fiddler rather than a place.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Possum Up a Gum Stump
tunes_named_for_city.notes: From the Long Island Museum's Mount manuscripts; performed on Mount's 1857 'Cradle of Harmony' fiddle by Matthew Christian.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Zip Coon / Turkey in the Straw
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Published c.1834 and popularized by New York blackface performer George Washington Dixon; Dan Bryant of Bryant's Minstrels (New York) copyrighted a 'Turkey in the Straw' in 1861 with the Zip Coon melody attached, which gave the tune its modern name.
tunes_named_for_city.ny_association: origin on the New York stage

tunes_named_for_city.title: Dixie
tunes_named_for_city.tradition: minstrel song, fiddle and band standard
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed in New York by fiddler Dan Emmett; first performed by Bryant's Minstrels at Mechanics' Hall, New York, April 4, 1859.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Oh, Dem Golden Slippers
tunes_named_for_city.notes: By James A. Bland (1879), born on Long Island in 1854 to free Black parents; he copyrighted only 35 of his hundreds of songs.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Flowers of Brooklyn
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed by Brooklyn-born accordionist Billy McComiskey (NEA Heritage Fellow 2016); on his Green Linnet LP 'Makin' the Rounds'; in 115 tunebooks on The Session.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Bonkers in Yonkers
tunes_named_for_city.notes: By Joanie Madden of Yonkers (Cherish the Ladies), on their album 'Woman of the House', played in B-flat. | Joanie Madden; played in B-flat by Cherish the Ladies.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Rockaway Beach
tunes_named_for_city.notes: From the playing of accordionist John Whelan, probably his own composition (per The Session); presumably the Queens beach. | From John Whelan's playing; probably his composition.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Train to Harlem

tunes_named_for_city.title: Washington Square Park
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed by box player Angus Lyon and fiddler Ruaridh Campbell (album '18 Months Later'); in 103 tunebooks on The Session.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Caucus Reel ('The Caucus at Secaucus')
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed in 1991 by Canadian flutist Jean Duval for the Comhaltas convention in Secaucus, NJ; notated from New Jersey flute player Mike Rafferty (Harker's collection).

tunes_named_for_city.title: Jersey Lightning
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Also 'Jersey Lightning Jig'; the name refers to New Jersey applejack. No composer found. | Named for New Jersey applejack.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Providence (the 'New York' jig turned waltz)

tunes_named_for_city.title: Fairytale of New York

fiddle_angle.topic: The first great body of evidence: enslaved fiddlers
fiddle_angle.detail: Nearly 100 fiddlers appear among the runaways in colonial and Revolutionary New York and New Jersey newspaper ads (Hodges & Brown, Pretends to Be Free).

Almack's, Five Points, 1842: 'The corpulent black fiddler, and his friend who plays the tambourine, stamp upon the boarding of the small raised orchestra... Instantly the fiddler grins, and goes at it tooth and nail.'

fiddle_angle.topic: The minstrel string band is born on the Bowery
fiddle_angle.detail: Feb 6, 1843: Dan Emmett (fiddle), Billy Whitlock (banjo), Frank Brower (bones), Dick Pelham (tambourine). 'Zip Coon' (c.1834) and 'Dixie' (1859) both come off the New York stage.

fiddle_angle.topic: William Sidney Mount, painter-fiddler of Long Island
fiddle_angle.detail: Kept manuscripts of hundreds of tunes (some dated and sourced: 'Merry Girls of New York', 1849; his own 'In the Cars on the Long Island Railroad', 1850; 'Shep Jones Hornpipe', 1854); patented the hollow-back 'Cradle of Harmony' violin (June 1, 1852) to cut through dance-floor noise; brother Robert Nelson Mount was a country fiddler and itinerant dancing master; uncle Micah Hawkins played violin. Mount's paintings (Rustic Dance After a Sleigh Ride, Dance of the Haymakers, Right and Left) are the best visual record of antebellum Northern dance fiddling, Black and white.

fiddle_angle.topic: New York as the fiddle-recording capital, 1916-1930s
fiddle_angle.detail: Columbia's first Irish dance records (1916, via O'Byrne DeWitt); Michael Coleman (1921-36, ~80 sides), James Morrison, Paddy Killoran; Eck Robertson (Victor, June 30-July 1, 1922, first country records); Gid Tanner (Columbia, March 1924); Sid Harkreader with Uncle Dave Macon (Vocalion, July 1924); Posey Rorer with Charlie Poole (Columbia, July 1925); Pawlo Humeniuk (OKeh from Dec 1925); Abe Schwartz's klezmer orchestras. Southern fiddle styles were often first recorded in Manhattan, and Sligo fiddling was exported back to Ireland from Manhattan studios.

Coleman (d. 1945, buried St. Raymond's, Bronx), Morrison (1918 New York Feis winner, teacher of hundreds), Killoran; then New York-raised heirs such as Andy McGann (Bronx; taught by Catherine Brennan Grant, played with Coleman), Longford-born Sligo-style fiddler Paddy Reynolds, and Brian Conway (1986 senior All-Ireland champion) and his pupils.
Martin Mulvihill (west Limerick; NEA 1984) taught Bronx children including Eileen Ivers; Larry Redican (Roscommon) mined Ryan's and Cole's for tunes and composed.

Michael Herman came to New York in 1930 to study violin, led World's Fair folk dancing (1940) and recorded hundreds of folk and contra dance tracks with his own orchestra (violin, Mary Ann on piano, Walter Erickson accordion) for the Folk Dancer label.

fiddle_angle.topic: Revival old-time fiddlers born or made in New York
fiddle_angle.detail: Mike Seeger and Tom Paley (NLCR, 1958), Wisconsin-raised Peter Stampfel (Holy Modal Rounders, Lower East Side, 1963), Kenny Kosek (Bronx, 1949), Jay Ungar (Bronx, 1946; 'Ashokan Farewell'), Bruce Molsky (NYC, 1955). FOTM brought Gaither Carlton (1961) and Fiddlin' Arthur Smith (1965) to New York stages.
Abe Schwartz (Romanian-born violinist, Columbia bandleader) to Alicia Svigals (Klezmatics); NEA Fellow Simon Shaheen (1994) plays oud and violin.

Harding's All-Round Collection of Jigs, Reels and Country Dances (Harding's Music House, New York; 1905 edition on IMSLP) was the city's main fiddle-tune book. The famous 'Ryan's Mammoth' was Boston (Howe), 'Cole's 1000' Chicago and 'O'Neill's' Chicago, not New York. Tin Pan Alley (from c.1885) published songs rather than fiddle collections.
Documented early contest: the New York Feis fiddle competition (Morrison won in 1918). No 1920s Ford-style old-time fiddle contest in the metro was found in this pass.

Heritage events are often free (Central Park rumba, casita jams, Lenape powwow); Shinnecock Powwow $20; Thunderbird Queens Farm powwow $12-19. Festivals: Brooklyn Folk Festival $165 pass or $75/day; Washington Square Park Folk Festival and Porch Stomp free.
