surprises: The first Comhaltas Ceoltoiri Eireann branch in North America was founded in Mineola, Long Island, in 1972-73 (Louis Quinn Branch, now Mulligan-Quinn), and the first US qualifying fleadh was held in the same hall. https://www.irishamericansociety.org/cce-mulligan-quinn-comhaltas

New York standardized Irish music for Ireland: most 1920s Irish 78s were cut in the New York area, and ITMA says their repertoire became 'a de facto national standard that persists in Ireland to this day'. https://newyork.itma.ie/recording-age/

The first country fiddle records were made in Manhattan, not the South: Eck Robertson cut 'Arkansaw Traveler' and 'Sallie Gooden' for Victor in New York on June 30-July 1, 1922, and Gid Tanner, Uncle Dave Macon, Ernest Stoneman and Charlie Poole all made their first records here in 1924-25. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eck_Robertson

Long Island's most famous 19th-century painter, William Sidney Mount, was a working dance fiddler who patented a hollow-backed 'Cradle of Harmony' violin (June 1, 1852); at the 1853 Crystal Palace the judges declared every violin entered 'unfit for competition'. https://www.bgc.bard.edu/about/news/618/01-jun-2017-a-cradle-of-harmony-at-the-crystal-palace

The fiddle-banjo-bones-tambourine minstrel band, ancestor of the string band, debuted on the Bowery on Feb 6, 1843 (Virginia Minstrels, Dan Emmett on fiddle); a year earlier Dickens watched a Five Points fiddler 'go at it tooth and nail'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Minstrels

For all Brooklyn's old-time revival image, bluegrass jams outnumber old-time jams about 71 to 15 a month across the metro, and the five boroughs' old-time circuit is mostly Monday nights. https://nybluegrass.com/

New York City's only square-dance club is LGBTQ+: Times Squares (founded 1984) calls itself the city's only square dance club and the country's largest LGBT-and-friends club. https://timessquares.nyc/

Inside the MSA's Pine Barrens corner, Albert Music Hall has held a show every Saturday night since November 1974, grown from two Sayreville brothers' 1950s hunting-cabin jams (George Albert on fiddle). https://www.alberthall.org/timeline

Bulgarian performers recorded by CTMD's founders Martin Koenig and Ethel Raim are on the Voyager Golden Record, so a Manhattan folk-arts nonprofit's field recordings are in interstellar space. https://www.arts.gov/honors/heritage/ethel-raim

Cherish the Ladies began as a 1985 one-off concert of immigrants' daughters for the Ethnic Folk Arts Center (now CTMD) and in 2026 became the first US-based group to win TG4's Gradam Ceoil group award. https://www.irishecho.com/2026/9/cherish-the-ladies-to-get-gradam-award

NYC's Cabaret Law killed the Eagle Tavern's Friday ceilis in the 1980s, capped unlicensed rooms at three musicians with no wind instruments, and its no-dancing rule lasted until 2017. https://newyork.itma.ie/revival-years/eagle-tavern-blarney-star/

Staten Island's monthly shanty session meets inside Sailors' Snug Harbor, the old sailors' retirement home where its namesake William Main Doerflinger collected shanties from the residents. https://noblemaritime.org/public

New Jersey sits at the root of shape-note singing (The Easy Instructor, 1801, co-compiled by a Hopewell man), and Great Migration Black singers held Sacred Harp singings in Newark and Vauxhall with the Colored Sacred Harp into the 1970s. http://lowereastsidesing.vocis.com/A%20Deep%20Rooted%20Tradition%20Returns%20Shape%20Note%20Music%20and%20Sacred%20Harp%20Singing%20in%20NJ%20+%20coronation.pdf

WFUV, the city's public music station, has no weekly folk show left (Woody's Children ended 2023 after 54 years; Sunday Supper ended Feb 15, 2026), yet its student-hosted Irish show Ceol na nGael has run every Sunday since 1974. https://wfuv.org/content/sunday-supper-february-15

COVID grew New Jersey's Folk Project: membership up 66% to 500 and $140,000 raised for performers; its Friday series began in 1975 in a restaurant basement with cable reels for tables and $1 admission. https://morristowngreen.com/2025/07/24/still-singing-after-all-these-years-the-troubadour-turns-50/

In the 1990s police confiscated Central Park's Sunday rumba drums, and for about two years the rumberos kept playing on their bodies, benches and beer coolers; the rumba, begun in the 1960s, still runs. https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/central-park-rumba-dancing-with-memory.htm

The word 'hootenanny' came to New York from Nate's corner of the country: Seeger and Guthrie picked it up at 1941 Washington Commonwealth Federation fund-raisers in Seattle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hootenanny

Thesession.org's New York database is mostly a graveyard: about 40 live MSA sessions against roughly 90 dead listings (closed bars, a pub burned in Hurricane Sandy, an owner who switched to rock). https://thesession.org/sessions/search?q=New+York,+USA
curiosities: Irish density: New York has 78-141 Irish session-nights a month depending on the confidence cut. Per Irish-ancestry resident, is that denser or thinner than Boston, Philadelphia or Chicago?

Bluegrass outnumbers old-time about 5 to 1 here (71 vs 15 jam-nights a month). Is that ratio typical of East Coast metros, and is it reversed in Seattle, Portland or the Bay Area where old-time is strong?

Contra runs about 9 dances a month for 20 million people (under 0.5 per million). How does contra-per-million compare with Boston, Seattle and the Bay Area, and is hall rent (Brooklyn Contra's stated constraint) the binding limit everywhere?
CDNY's English country dance is weekly but its contra is not. Is ECD stronger than contra in the other old CDSS centers (Boston, Philadelphia), or is this a New York peculiarity of the 1915 lineage?

Paid leaders look normal here (mic'd house sessions at the Dead Rabbit and Swift, a $15 suggested donation at Mary O's, a $10 old-time learning jam that pays its leader). Do other cities pay session or jam leaders, and does it change who joins?
Did New York's Cabaret Law (no social dancing without a licence until 2017) suppress participatory dance in NYC compared with cities that never had such a law?
What is the median lifespan of a pub session? About 90 dead NY-area listings on thesession suggest 2-5 year churn; is it shorter than in lower-rent cities?
Craft breweries now host many NJ and Brooklyn jams (Conclave, Flounder, Descendants, Grimm, Forever). Is the taproom jam a national post-2015 pattern replacing pubs and church halls?
Sacred Harp: the 2026 NYC All-Day drew 177 registered singers. How does that compare with all-days in Chicago, Boston, the Bay Area and Seattle (fasola.org minutes could answer this)?
The Seaport's chantey sing is 50+ years old. Which other port cities (Boston, Baltimore, San Francisco, Seattle) have museum-hosted monthly sings, and did the 2021 TikTok shanty boom lift attendance?
Public stations are dropping folk shows (WFUV 2023 and 2026) while college and Pacifica stations (WFDU, WKCR, WBAI) keep theirs. Is that a national pattern?

The Folk Project grew to 500 members after COVID while the Folk Music Society of Huntington stopped presenting. What predicts survival for suburban folk societies: pricing, streaming, owned halls, or dance plus concerts under one roof?
CTMD has worked with 20 NEA Heritage Fellows and spun off seven organizations. Does any other metro have a single folk-arts nonprofit with that reach, and how do Heritage Fellows per capita compare?
Bomba has a weekly class circuit here (LP21 Mondays and Tuesdays, Bombazo Saturdays). Which city has more weekly bomba: New York, Orlando, Chicago or Philadelphia?
Cape Breton fiddling barely registers in New York but thrived in Boston. Did Cape Bretoners here assimilate into the Irish scene, or never arrive in numbers?
How many fiddle records were cut in New York studios versus Atlanta, Bristol and Chicago in 1922-32? DAHR session data could test the 'New York as fiddle-recording capital' claim.
data_quality_notes: Merged from five research threads (irish-celtic, oldtime-dance, song-listening, heritage, history-archives), all run Oct 2026 under heavy search rate limits, so most evidence is from primary pages (venue and society sites, the FMSNY Oct 2026 newsletter, the nybluegrass.com Google Calendar, NJ's 'All Jam No Spam' PDF, CTMD's events archive, NEA pages, ITMA) plus listings and social-post snippets. Method: name-based dedup (74 automatic merges) plus manual drops of cross-thread duplicates (Brooklyn Traditional Slow Jam, NYC Tanchaz, Golden Festival, Porch Stomp, several archives, people, defunct venues and tunes) and of recurring events with no dated 2024-26 evidence (Lowlands old-time jam, Rockland Contra, Shmulik Gov-Ari Israeli sessions, Monmouth Folk Dancers, Rumberos United, Buckley's 2022 session) or that are one-offs or schools rather than recurring events (BKCM square dance, Ukrainian Village Voices rehearsals with no published cadence, Cumbe's ~30 commercial classes a month, Mariachi Academy's youth classes); the schools remain under instruction. Listings dated for Nov-Dec 2026 were capped to last_evidence 2026-10. Out-of-MSA items (Princeton/Mercer, Beacon/Dutchess, East Durham, Pawling, Howell Farm, Newtown PA) are flagged and excluded from headline stats. Confidence: totals include low-confidence listings. All events sum to about 410 event-nights a month; medium/high-confidence only, about 324. Irish sessions: 140.6/month across 43 listings, but only 6 have current official (high-confidence) evidence and 17 are low (MurphGuide June 2024, a single thesession post, or word of mouth); the medium/high figure, 77.8, is the safer number, and it includes mic'd listen-only house sessions. Bluegrass (71.3; 61.6 medium/high) comes mostly from a volunteer calendar whose open-ended entries may outlive real jams; seasonal jams (Gowanus Dredgers, Postcrypt) are counted at in-season rates. About 29/month in category 'other' are listening series and dance-party nights, not participatory sessions. Heritage events (34/month) are undercounted: many heritage traditions run on annual feasts, parades and private gatherings rather than public weekly events. festivals_active (50) is broad: it includes parades, feasts and heritage festivals as well as folk festivals; three uncertain ones were set to hiatus or dropped. distinct_traditions_active was recomputed by hand: the merge's free-text count (140) was inflated by spelling variants, so it is replaced by 69 named traditions with documented 2024-26 practice: 24 Anglo-Celtic-American instrumental, dance and song forms from the events census, plus 45 heritage traditions the heritage thread rated thriving, active or niche (excluding fading Cantonese opera and Cambodian music, historic-only forms, classical South Asian dance, and the museum Pinkster recreation); about half of the heritage ratings rest on one or two sources. Blocked or unreadable: Facebook and most Instagram pages, litma.org (corporate filter), tunearch.org (Cloudflare), the Ceol Agus Rince ceili calendar (so monthly ceilis are undercounted), citylore.org, NYT (paywall). Sources disagree on: the Irish Arts Center building opening (Dec 2021, not 2023), Gaelic Park (1926 vs 1928), the NJ Irish Festival ('since 1971' vs 53rd in 2025), KlezKamp's last year (2014 vs 2015), the 2026 Mid-Atlantic Fleadh site (Princeton vs Plainsboro), LITMA's contra Sunday (2nd vs 3rd), the Staten Island song circle (4th Wednesday vs Saturday), Folk Dance House's 16th Street date (1940s vs 1951), Humeniuk's sales (100,000 vs 150,000) and Brooklyn Folk Festival edition numbers. No attendance or demographic surveys were found for any scene. Borough/county splits in the dossier come from a place-name heuristic and are approximate. Not researched in depth: Staten Island and the Bronx beyond a few listings, Irish step-dance schools and pipe bands, Jamaican, Ethiopian, Nigerian, Bangladeshi and Punjabi traditions, current Cantonese opera clubs.
